subject: Banking
title: Why Companies Merge
description: Learn Why Companies Merge in one minute.

hook.text: When Exxon merged with Mobil in 1999, the combined company dominated global oil. Mergers create power through scale.

buildup.text: Companies merge to cut costs, expand markets, acquire technology, or eliminate competitors.

discovery.text: The buyer usually pays a premium over the target's market price.

twist.text: Studies show 60-70% of mergers destroy value for the acquiring company.

climax.text: Mergers are often driven by CEO ambition as much as strategy.

punchline.text: 60-70% of mergers destroy value. Size tempts more than logic.

quiz.question: What percentage of mergers destroy value for the acquiring company?

details.summary: Companies merge to gain market share, acquire technology or talent, achieve cost savings through economies of scale, enter new markets, or eliminate competitors. Strategic rationale varies, but growth pressure is the constant driver.
details.whyItMatters: Mergers reshape entire industries, affecting employees, consumers, and competitors. Understanding the real motivations behind mergers reveals that shareholder value creation is often secondary to empire-building ambitions.
takeaways: Synergy promises drive most merger justifications to shareholders
Studies show the majority of mergers fail to create the promised value
CEO ego and empire building often motivate acquisitions more than strategy

faq.question: Do most mergers actually succeed?
faq.answer: Research consistently shows that 60 to 80 percent of mergers fail to create the synergies and value promised. Cultural clashes, integration failures, and overpayment destroy value more often than mergers create it.

faq.question: What does synergy really mean in a merger?
faq.answer: Synergy means the combined company is worth more than the two separate companies. In practice, this usually means cutting duplicate costs like offices and staff. Revenue synergies, where the combined company sells more, rarely materialize.
